People analytics · Tier A diagnostic + predictive

11 of this file's 27 attrition drivers are indistinguishable from random numbers

A driver analysis and early-warning model for the IBM HR employee-attrition dataset, built around a control the file supplies by accident: three columns of verified noise.

1,470 employees · 237 leavers (16.1%) · single cross-sectional snapshot · prepared 27 July 2026

Situation · Complication · Resolution

Situation. IBM's HR attrition file is the most-used teaching dataset in people analytics: 1,470 employees, 35 columns, zero missing values, and a clean 16.1% attrition label. Hundreds of published notebooks analyse it, and they converge on the same driver list — overtime, low pay, long commutes, poor work-life balance.

Complication. Three of its compensation columns are random numbers. DailyRate, HourlyRate and MonthlyRate correlate with actual pay at |ρ| < 0.06, are statistically indistinguishable from uniform draws, and describe no employee's earnings. Yet DailyRate scores 0.545 against attrition — higher than work-life balance — and survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q = 0.048. Meanwhile the pay gap that anchors most write-ups turns out to be 90% explained by job level rather than by pay (VIF 6.5), and the engagement fields that make these models look good may have been collected on the way out the door.

Once the file is made to supply its own noise floor, 11 of 27 candidate attrition drivers cannot be told apart from a random column — including work-life balance, promotion gap, training and performance rating — and the pay gap dissolves into job level; what survives is a short list led by overtime, on which an HRIS-only score catches 70% of leavers by calling 29% of the workforce, without ever touching the engagement survey.

Key line 1 · INSTRUMENT

Six of 35 columns carry no information, and three of them are dressed as pay data — which makes them the most useful thing in the file.

Retained as a calibrated placebo control rather than deleted, the three random columns show what noise can manufacture at this sample size: a ceiling of 0.545 univariate AUC. Measured against it, 11 of 27 real candidate drivers fail — among them PerformanceRating (0.501, exactly chance), WorkLifeBalance (0.536) and PercentSalaryHike (0.518). FDR correction alone was not enough: it promoted DailyRate itself to "significant".

Key line 2 · LEVERS

What survives is short, and pay is not on it — overtime is the one lever that dominates every test.

Employees working overtime leave at 30.5% against 10.4%, in all three departments, with the largest effect size in the file (Cramér's V = 0.24) and roughly double the odds after adjustment for role, level, tenure and travel. It is also the single most load-bearing column in the fitted model — scrambling it costs 0.201 PR-AUC, 3.4× the next-largest column. Pay behaves differently: the widely-quoted 38% median gap between leavers and stayers collapses to 10% within Job Level 1, because income is 90% explained by level.

Key line 3 · LIMITS

An HRIS-only score is good enough to act on and honest about what it cannot do — but it flags single employees 2.8× as often as divorced ones, and deleting the column does not fix it.

Scope 1 reaches 0.553 PR-AUC in cross-validation against a 0.161 floor (0.510 on the held-out set, 95% CI [0.37, 0.65]), and it is well calibrated (Brier 0.102 against 0.135 for a base-rate model), so risk tiers are supportable. Adding the engagement survey buys +0.102 PR-AUC — but that lift has two indistinguishable explanations, genuine signal or post-decision reporting, and a snapshot cannot separate them. The marital-status disparity survives removing the column, because StockOptionLevel reconstructs marital status at 0.94 AUC.

Recommendation — for the HR analytics lead

  1. Retire the noise-band tiles from the attrition dashboard this quarter. PerformanceRating, PercentSalaryHike, TrainingTimesLastYear, WorkLifeBalance and YearsSinceLastPromotion cannot be distinguished from a random column on this data. Redirect the retention budget to the four levers that survive: overtime load, business travel, stock-option coverage, and the first-year Level-1 cohort.
  2. Build the early-warning score on HRIS fields only. It reaches 0.553 PR-AUC against a 0.161 floor, runs monthly for every employee rather than quarterly for survey respondents, and is well calibrated (Brier 0.102) so risk tiers are supportable. At the recommended threshold it flags 344 of 1,176 employees to catch 133 of 190 leavers — 2.6 conversations per leaver found. Use the engagement survey to explain a flag, never to produce one.
  3. Manage the marital-status disparity where the list is used, not in the feature set. Deleting the column moves the 2.83× flag-rate gap only to 2.64×, because StockOptionLevel reconstructs marital status at 0.94 AUC. Monitor flag rates by group, review outreach lists before they are actioned, and disclose the disparity to whoever acts on them.
  4. Instrument the HRIS before anyone attempts a causal claim. Capture hire date, exit date, exit reason and manager ID. Every question worth asking next — does cutting overtime reduce attrition, do specific managers drive exits, when in the lifecycle do people decide — is unanswerable from a snapshot, and no modelling effort substitutes for the four fields that are missing.

Scope note. This is a diagnostic and predictive study (rungs 2 and 4 of the analytics ladder). Causal inference is out of scope and no causal claim is made: the file is a single snapshot with no event dates and no assignment mechanism, so every finding below is an association. The dataset is IBM's synthetic demonstration file, so the transferable output is the method — noise calibration, scope quarantine, confound decomposition — and the instrumentation recommendation, not the coefficients.

Part I · Instrument

What this file can and cannot support

Before asking which characteristics drive attrition, it is worth asking what this data is capable of showing. The answer turned out to be less than it appears — and the reason is visible in the file itself.

Three of this file's compensation columns are random numbers — and that makes them the most useful thing in it

Four independent tests: implied hours-per-day and days-per-month ratios spread 12–24× between the 5th and 95th percentile; |ρ| < 0.06 against every other column; uniformity cannot be rejected; and the observed AUC sits inside the label-shuffle null.

So what: a dataset that hands you a proven-random column hands you a free calibration standard. Deleting these three at cleaning time — the obvious move — would have thrown away the only way to tell a weak real signal from a strong-looking accident. DailyRate reaches p = 0.030 against attrition; keeping it is what stopped it being published as a driver.

11 of 27 candidate attrition drivers cannot beat a column of random numbers

Every feature scored against its own permutation null (2,000 label shuffles; 400 for nominal features, scored out-of-fold). The shaded band is what 23 columns known to be random actually reached.

So what: the failures are not obscure fields. PerformanceRating, PercentSalaryHike, TrainingTimesLastYear, WorkLifeBalance and YearsSinceLastPromotion are standing items on attrition dashboards. Tracking them costs analyst time and, where a retention budget follows the dashboard, spends money against a random number.

The full verdict table

Each feature tested against its own permutation null, then Benjamini–Hochberg corrected across all 30 columns, then checked against the ceiling that 23 known-random columns actually reached. DRIVER requires clearing both bars; MARGINAL means significant but inside the range noise can manufacture; INERT means indistinguishable from a shuffled label.

Why the third criterion exists. FDR correction alone flagged 19 of 30 columns as significant — including DailyRate, which we had already proven to be a uniform random draw. That is the false-discovery rate working exactly as specified: at q < 0.05 across 30 tests, roughly one false positive is the price of admission. Normally you never learn which one it is. Here we do, and that is the entire argument for keeping proven-noise columns in the analysis rather than deleting them at cleaning time.

Part II · Levers

What survives, and what it is worth

Overtime is the one lever that survives every test — 30.5% attrition against 10.4%, in every department

Cramér's V = 0.24, the largest effect in the file; odds ratio ≈ 2.1 after adjustment for role, level, tenure, travel and distance; and the largest permutation importance in the fitted model by a factor of three.

So what: this is the finding to fund. It is measured from a field the HRIS already holds, it holds in every department, and it survives adjustment. The caveat is causal, not statistical: a snapshot cannot tell whether overtime pushes people out or whether people on the way out are the ones assigned it. Treat it as the highest-priority place to run a controlled test, not as a proven cause.

The 38% pay gap between leavers and stayers is a seniority effect — within Level 1 it is 10%

MonthlyIncome is 90% explained by JobLevel (R²). Conditioning on level, the gap reverses sign at Levels 2 and 5.

So what: "raise pay to retain people" is not supported here. Leavers earn less because leavers are junior. A within-level pay effect does survive (OR 0.45, 95% CI [0.25, 0.80]) but it lives entirely in the top pay quartile, and it is dwarfed by level itself (OR 0.58 per step). An across-the-board raise sized off the headline gap would be expensive and aimed at the wrong mechanism.

Attrition is a first-year, entry-level phenomenon — 34.9% in year one against 8.1% after a decade

Wilson 95% intervals. 143 of 237 leavers sit in Job Level 1; 162 have five years' tenure or less.

So what: a retention budget spread evenly across 1,470 employees is spread across the wrong people. The at-risk cohort can be named, counted and targeted from fields the HRIS already holds — no survey, no model, no new instrumentation required.

Sales Representatives leave at 39.8% — sixteen times the rate of Research Directors

Wilson 95% intervals, which is why the small roles are shown wide: Human Resources (n = 52) spans 13–37%.

So what: target Sales Representatives with confidence — n = 83 and the whole interval sits above the company average. Treat the small-role rankings as a watchlist rather than a finding; on 52 employees, a rank is not a result.

Overtime and stock options carry the largest actionable effects; every engagement field is smaller

Rank-biserial r for ordered features, Cramér's V for nominal ones, 2,000-resample bootstrap intervals. Diamonds mark the proven-random controls.

So what: significance ranks career-stage variables first, but effect size re-orders the list toward the two things the organisation actually sets — overtime and stock options. Age and tenure are context for targeting; they are not levers.

Part III · Limits

What a model built on the survivors can do — and what it costs

Every model family lands within 0.22 PR-AUC of the others — the ceiling is the data, not the algorithm

25 stratified CV fits per configuration. Majority-class baseline 0.162; best single feature 0.228.

So what: there is no algorithm win available. Gradient boosting, random forests and SVMs do not beat a logistic regression here. Effort spent on model selection is wasted; the binding constraint is what the HRIS records, which is why the fourth recommendation is about instrumentation rather than modelling.

The engagement survey adds +0.102 PR-AUC — and what it adds cannot be told apart from leakage

Identical model and pipeline in both scopes; only the input columns change.

So what: build the score on HRIS fields alone. It runs monthly for every employee instead of quarterly for survey respondents, it cannot be contaminated by answers given after someone has already decided to leave, and it gives up little. The survey's real value is diagnostic — explaining why a flagged employee is at risk — not predictive.

Catching 70% of leavers means calling 344 of 1,176 employees — 2.6 conversations per leaver found

Threshold 0.196, chosen on training folds against a stated cost frame and confirmed once on the held-out set.

So what: this is the number the decision actually turns on. Pushing to 90% recall would mean calling 742 employees — nearly two-thirds of the workforce — to catch 38 more leavers. The recall/headcount curve, not the AUC, is what an HR director should be shown.

The model flags single employees 2.8× as often as divorced ones — statistically correct, and a protected-adjacent disparity

Out-of-fold predictions over all 1,470 employees at the chosen threshold. Gender shows no meaningful gap in flag rate, recall or AUC.

So what: deleting MaritalStatus does not fix this. The other HRIS columns reconstruct it at 0.94 AUC — StockOptionLevel alone carries most of it — so the disparity barely moves (2.83× to 2.64×) when the column is removed. This has to be managed where the list is used, not where the features are chosen.

The exposure in this model is marital status, which is the one most audits do not check.

Appendix

Methodology & technical detail

Data lineage

WA_Fn-UseC_-HR-Employee-Attrition.csv (1,470 × 35, SHA-256 logged at ingestion) → schema validation, 32 rules across three families, 0 failures → hr_clean.parquet (1,470 × 33) → diagnostic and modelling outputs. Raw data is never edited after ingestion. Every number in this report is read from JSON written by notebooks 02, 04 and 05; none is typed in by hand.

What was dropped, and why

  • EmployeeCount, Over18, StandardHours — zero variance, one value across all 1,470 rows.
  • DailyRate, HourlyRate, MonthlyRate — retained in the data and in the model matrix, but excluded from every finding and labelled role = placebo. They are the calibration standard, not features.
  • Department — dropped from the multivariate specification only. Job role predicts department for 96.7% of employees, and including both caused quasi-separation and a non-converging fit.

Measurement-scale contract

Fixed once at cleaning time and persisted to disk, so no downstream notebook re-decides it. Two calls were made on evidence rather than habit: BusinessTravel is treated as ordinal because the response is monotonic (8.0% → 15.0% → 24.9%), while StockOptionLevel is treated as nominal because it is not (24.4% → 9.4% → 7.6% → 17.6%) — fitting a line through that U-shape would report the wrong sign for the level-3 group.

Statistical protocol

  • Tests. Mann–Whitney U with rank-biserial r for ordered features (normality rejected for every numeric column, Shapiro p < 0.001); χ² with Cramér's V for nominal ones. All effect sizes carry 2,000-resample bootstrap intervals.
  • Null distribution. Per-feature permutation, 2,000 label shuffles for ordered features and 400 for nominal ones. Nominal features are scored out-of-fold under group-rate encoding so that a nine-level category cannot buy separation with cardinality alone.
  • Multiple comparisons. Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q < 0.05 across all 30 columns, plus the noise-ceiling criterion described in Part I.
  • Collinearity. MonthlyIncome ~ JobLevel R² = 0.903; maximum VIF in the reported specification 20. Career-stage variables are interpreted as a block, never as independent effects.

Modelling protocol

  • Split. Stratified 80/20. The training set (1,176 employees) carries all model selection, ablation and threshold choice via RepeatedStratifiedKFold(5×5) — 25 fits per configuration. The held-out set (294 employees, 47 leavers) was touched exactly once.
  • Scope quarantine. Scope 1 never sees an engagement field at any stage, including feature selection. Scope 2 adds the five Likert fields and is reported only as a comparator.
  • Model selection. On PR-AUC, declared before any model was fitted. Winner: 1b · Logistic (unweighted). Class weighting was tested and not used — it did not improve ranking and would have cost calibration; the decision threshold is set explicitly instead.
  • Derived features. All ten proposed in the data assessment were built inside the pipeline and ablation-tested as a block. They changed PR-AUC by -0.0062 against a fold-to-fold standard deviation of roughly 0.07, so they were dropped. The negative result is reported rather than buried.
  • Held-out result. PR-AUC 0.510 (95% CI [0.367, 0.655]), ROC-AUC 0.789 (95% CI [0.708, 0.866]). The intervals are wide because 47 leavers is a small number; the cross-validated estimate is the headline and this is the sanity check.

Appendix exhibits

Predicted risk tracks observed risk — Brier 0.102 against 0.135 for a base-rate model, so risk tiers are supportable

In-model importance, with the three proven-random columns as a zero line — OverTime is load-bearing; MaritalStatus and JobLevel rank below a placebo because the rest of the matrix reconstructs them

Limitations

  • Synthetic data. This is IBM's demonstration file, not a real workforce. The coefficients describe a generator, not an organisation. What transfers is the method and the instrumentation recommendation.
  • No time dimension. No hire date, exit date or snapshot date, so survival and hazard models are unavailable and no causal design is possible. Using YearsAtCompany as a time proxy would be weaker and less defensible than the classifier reported here.
  • Direction of effect is unidentified. Overtime is the strongest association in the file, but a snapshot cannot say whether it pushes people out or whether people already leaving are the ones assigned it.
  • Engagement fields may be post-decision. The data assessment cannot rule out that satisfaction was recorded at or near exit. This is why they are quarantined, and why the +0.102 PR-AUC they add is reported with two explanations rather than one.
  • Small positive class. 237 leavers overall, 47 in the held-out set. Every interval in this report is wide for that reason and is shown rather than rounded away.
  • Not deployable. No monitoring, no drift plan, no external validation, and a protected-adjacent flag-rate disparity that cannot be removed by feature selection.

Tier A gate checklist

  • SCR finalised and evidence-backed; governing thought is one sentence answering the business question
  • Key lines are MECE — instrument, findings, limits — and jointly cover every analysis run
  • Executive summary passes the one-page test: the recommendation is on page one with its quantified basis
  • Every exhibit carries an action title and a "So What" in business language
  • Effect sizes with bootstrap intervals reported alongside every p-value; FDR correction applied
  • Null results reported as findings — 11 inert or marginal features named, not omitted
  • Model compared against majority-class and single-feature baselines; accuracy explicitly disqualified
  • Fairness audit executed with per-subgroup intervals, proxy test, and the measured cost of mitigation
  • Methodology in the appendix, not the narrative; all code reproducible with pinned dependencies and a fixed seed
